strengths: Strong and consistent quantitative results: PercHead outperforms LGM, PanoHead, GAGAvatar, and LAM on PSNR, LPIPS, DreamSim, and ArcFace distance on both Ava-256 and NeRSemble, and the gains are particularly large in the extreme-view setting (e.g., PSNR 15.58 vs 14.16 for PanoHead on Ava-256), which is the paper's stated core challenge.

The perceptual loss formulation using DINOv2 and SAM2.1 features is well motivated and validated by a clean ablation (Table 3) that compares 2D-only data, multi-view-only data, LPIPS+L1, DINOv2-only, SAM2.1-only, and the full configuration, isolating the contribution of the proposed supervision.

The paper demonstrates a genuinely useful downstream capability: disentangled 3D head editing controlled independently by segmentation maps (geometry) and CLIP image/text embeddings (style), including zero-shot text-driven editing and a demonstrated interactive web GUI, which adds practical value beyond reconstruction.

The architectural design is sensible and clearly explained: dual-branch encoder (frozen DINOv2 + task-specific ViT), MAE-style 3D ViT decoder operating on FLAME-derived 3D patches with iterative cross-attention, and Gaussian Splatting rendering, with the 3D-patch decoder replacing expensive pixel-space transformers.

The paper shows frame-by-frame video generalization (Fig. 4) without additional fine-tuning, which is a non-trivial generalization result and supports the claim of 3D-consistent, temporally coherent reconstruction.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate and somewhat compositional: the method largely assembles existing components (FLAME template, MAE-style ViT decoder, frozen DINOv2, Gaussian Splatting, CLIP), and the primary conceptual novelty is the foundation-model perceptual loss, which is related to prior work using DINO features (e.g., [14, 39, 51, 61]) that the paper itself cites.

Baseline coverage is limited. Several relevant recent methods discussed in Related Work (e.g., Portrait4D, Portrait4Dv2, Arc2Avatar, and editing methods such as ClipFace) are not included in the quantitative comparison, so the claimed state-of-the-art status is only established against a subset of the relevant literature.

Evaluation breadth is narrow: quantitative results use only 11 identities from Ava-256 and 5 held-out identities from NeRSemble, and the evaluation protocol aligns crops to PanoHead's tightest crop, which may interact with the reported metrics in ways not fully analyzed.

The editing capability is evaluated only qualitatively (Figs. 5, 6, 9); there are no quantitative editing metrics, no comparison to editing baselines, and no user study, so the strength of the disentanglement and editing claims rests on selected visual examples.

The paper claims state-of-the-art but GAGAvatar actually achieves higher SSIM on both datasets and both view settings (0.7428 vs 0.7003, etc.); the authors dismiss SSIM as less perceptually aligned but do not provide a rigorous justification beyond citing DreamSim/ArcFace, leaving a metric where the method is not best.

Some architectural claims are not fully substantiated: the paper states that global coherence emerges entirely from the shared 2D feature context while omitting self-attention among 3D patches, but provides no analysis of when this independence breaks down (e.g., patches that must coordinate globally), and no ablation isolating the effect of removing 3D self-attention.

Reproducibility details are partial: the two-stage training schedule (70h base + 24h CNN refinement) is reported, but key hyperparameters (loss weighting between DINOv2 and SAM2.1, decoder depth, Gaussian count per patch) and the perceptual-loss normalization are not fully specified in the main text.

The training dataset is a hybrid of NeRSemble, Cafa, and FFHQ, while evaluation uses Ava-256 and held-out NeRSemble identities; the paper does not analyze potential domain overlap or how the hybrid data affects generalization, which could confound the reported cross-dataset gains.

strengths: Introduces a perceptually motivated supervision strategy based on frozen DINOv2 and SAM2.1 features, and the ablation (Table 3, Fig. 7) provides concrete evidence that this replaces conventional LPIPS+L1 supervision more effectively for 3D consistency and identity preservation — a genuinely useful and somewhat counter-intuitive empirical finding.

Strong and consistent quantitative gains on both novel-view and extreme-view reconstruction across two datasets (Ava-256, NeRSemble), outperforming LGM, PanoHead, GAGAvatar, and LAM on PSNR, LPIPS, DreamSim, and ArcFace, with the largest margins precisely in the difficult extreme-viewpoint regime that matters most for single-image lifting.

The framework is coherent and well-motivated: a shared 3D ViT decoder with cross-attention to 2D features, PixelShuffle-to-Gaussians, and a CNN refinement module, with a sensible two-phase training schedule. The decoder design choices (FLAME-based patch initialization, no self-attention among patches, foreground-only patches) are explicitly justified.

A meaningful extension to disentangled 3D editing is demonstrated, where geometry is controlled by segmentation maps and style by either a reference image or CLIP text embeddings, with qualitative evidence of geometry/style disentanglement (Figs. 5, 6) and a working interactive GUI described in the supplementary.

The paper is clearly written, the figures are informative, and the supplementary material (evaluation subjects, cropping alignment, GAGAvatar background normalization, decoder visualization protocol) is thorough and aids reproducibility.

Robustness to extreme viewing angles is a genuine and important contribution for immersive/avatar applications, and the qualitative comparison (Figs. 3, 8, 9) supports the claim that competing methods degrade sharply under large viewpoint changes.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is modest: the dual-branch encoder (DINOv2 + task ViT), the 3D ViT decoder, PixelShuffle-to-Gaussians, and Gaussian splatting pipeline draw heavily on LAM, GRM, GAGAvatar, and GAGAvatar's preprocessing. The primary novel component is the loss function, so the overall system reads as a well-engineered recombination rather than a fundamentally new method.

The core perceptual-loss idea — using foundation-model (e.g., DINO) features as a perceptual objective — has appeared in prior 2D and 3D work; combining DINOv2 with SAM2.1 is a reasonable but incremental extension, and the paper does not sufficiently position this against existing foundation-feature losses.

Editing capability is evaluated only qualitatively. There are no quantitative metrics for editing fidelity, style consistency, identity preservation under edits, or robustness of zero-shot text edits, making it difficult to substantiate the claimed strength of the disentanglement.

Evaluation breadth is limited: only 11 identities from Ava-256 and 5 held-out NeRSemble identities, and only four baselines. Several recent single-image 3D head methods (e.g., Portrait4D/Portrait4D-v2, Arc2Avatar, newer 2024/2025 Gaussian-head works) are not compared despite being directly relevant.

The method is bounded by a fixed FLAME-derived canonical topology (4,096 patches × 16 Gaussians) with no self-attention among 3D patches. This likely constrains geometric expressiveness (e.g., hair, accessories, non-template regions) and global coherence, and the paper does not analyze failure cases arising from this.

Practical limitations are significant and only briefly acknowledged: the editing pipeline takes ~25–30s per operation, lighting is baked into the reconstruction, and dynamic expression transfer is unsupported, which undercuts claims of usefulness for real-time avatar/telepresence scenarios.

The 'state-of-the-art' claim is qualified — GAGAvatar achieves higher SSIM in the novel-view setting — so the reported superiority is metric-dependent and would benefit from a clearer discussion of where the method does not dominate.

The zero-shot text editing relies solely on injecting a global CLIP token into the encoder, which typically offers coarse, weakly localized control; the paper does not probe the reliability or failure modes of this mechanism beyond a few curated examples.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and challenging problem—single-image 3D head reconstruction with downstream semantic editing—and delivers an end-to-end system that covers both lifting and editing.

Reports consistent improvements over the compared baselines (LGM, PanoHead, GAGAvatar, LAM) on perceptual metrics (LPIPS, DreamSim, ArcFace) across two datasets and two evaluation regimes (novel views and extreme views), which is a non-trivial empirical result.

The geometry/style disentanglement via a segmentation map for geometry plus CLIP embeddings (or reference images) for style is a sensible and reusable design, and the qualitative editing results (Figs. 5, 6) illustrate useful controllability.

The supplementary provides additional qualitative comparisons (Figs. 8, 9) and details of the evaluation protocol, and the use of foundation-model features as a perceptual signal is a reasonable direction.
Ablation over training data (2D-only vs multi-view-only) and loss variants (Table 3) is provided, showing that the multi-view + single-image mix helps.
weaknesses: The central claimed novelty—using DINOv2 and SAM2.1 features as perceptual supervision—is overstated. The paper itself cites prior work using foundation-model features for perceptual similarity (DreamSim [14], [39], [51], [61]), so this is an incremental variant rather than a new formulation. The abstract's framing of it as a 'novel perceptual supervision strategy' overreaches.

The architecture is largely an assembly of existing components: a DINOv2 + task-specific ViT dual encoder (from LAM [24]), a MAE-style decoder [23] with cross-attention over a FLAME template, PixelShuffle-to-Gaussians (from GRM [60]), and Gaussian Splatting [27]. The paper does not clearly isolate what is genuinely new in the architecture beyond combining these pieces.

The paper's core scientific claim—that replacing conventional reconstruction/perceptual losses (LPIPS, SSIM, L1) with foundation-model supervision yields better results—is not supported by its own ablation. In Table 3, 'LPIPS+L1 w.o. CNN' beats 'Full w.o. CNN' on PSNR (15.96 vs 15.94), SSIM (0.7228 vs 0.7089), and LPIPS (0.2897 vs 0.3010); the full model only wins on DS and ArcFace. The stated 'surprisingly effective' loss is therefore only marginally better and worse on several metrics.

The editing model, a headline contribution, is evaluated only qualitatively (Figs. 5, 6). There is no quantitative metric, no user study, and no comparison against editing baselines (e.g., ClipFace, LAM, InstructPix2NeRF). Given that the paper positions editing as a key capability, this is a material evidentiary gap.

Reported PSNR values are very low (≈15.6–18.0 dB) for image synthesis, which sits awkwardly with the repeated 'high-fidelity' and 'state-of-the-art' framing. The paper never contextualizes these numbers or explains why reconstruction quality is so low in absolute terms, making the fidelity claims hard to assess.

SSIM is worse than GAGAvatar on both novel-view and extreme-view evaluations on both datasets, and the paper dismisses this as SSIM being 'less aligned with human perception' without providing supporting evidence or a perceptual study to justify the dismissal.

The evaluation set is small: 11 identities from Ava-256 and 5 from NeRSemble. No more recent or stronger baselines (e.g., Portrait4D/Portrait4Dv2, IDEG, general 3D lifting methods such as LRM/TripoSR) are compared, limiting the strength of the state-of-the-art claim.
The video/frame-by-frame generalization claim (Fig. 4) is purely qualitative, with no temporal-consistency metrics, despite being presented as an important downstream capability.

Despite emphasizing Gaussian Splatting efficiency, no runtime, memory, or latency comparison against baselines is provided, so the efficiency motivation is unsubstantiated. (The supplementary gives only editing-time numbers for their own method.)

Presentation problems: the abstract is dense and difficult to parse, the 'Project Website:' field is left empty, and several strong claims ('state-of-the-art', 'exceptional robustness', 'significantly surpasses') are not matched by the magnitude of the reported gains or the scope of the evaluation.

strengths: Introduces a novel perceptual loss based on DINOv2 and SAM 2.1 foundation-model features that serves as a drop-in replacement for standard pixel-level losses (L1/LPIPS/SSIM), with thorough ablations (Fig. 9, 10, Tab. 2) showing it substantially improves supervision of high-frequency regions such as hair, glasses, and teeth, and yields better robustness under out-of-distribution inputs (Fig. 18).

Strong and consistent quantitative results on Ava-256 and NeRSemble, especially in the extreme-view setting, where the method achieves large improvements in LPIPS, DreamSim, and ArcFace over strong baselines (PanoHead, SphereHead, GAGAvatar, LAM, LGM), and where the improvement gap widens relative to baselines that degrade under large view changes (Tab. 1, Tab. 3).

Well-designed and informative ablation studies that isolate the contributions of the training-data mixture (2D-only vs. multi-view vs. combined), the loss formulation (LPIPS+L1, DINOv2, SAM2.1, combined), and the SHP-CNN sharpening module, providing actionable insight into why the proposed formulation works.

Demonstrates practical downstream value through disentangled 3D editing (geometry controlled by a segmentation map, style by text or reference image), with an interactive GUI and supplementary video, and shows zero-shot text editing via CLIP despite no text-specific training (Fig. 5, 6, 19, 20).

Reproducibility is supported by the release of training and inference code together with the interactive GUI on the project website, and the supplementary provides detailed training/architecture hyperparameters (epochs, optimizer, decoder dimensions, patch counts).
weaknesses: The core architecture is largely built on LAM: the dual-branch 2D encoder is explicitly described as augmenting LAM's approach, the 3D ViT decoder, cross-attention design, FLAME anchoring, and PixelShuffle Gaussian prediction closely follow that prior work. The primary architectural novelty is thus limited, and the main contribution reduces essentially to the loss formulation and the editing extension.

Quantitative evaluation of the editing model is essentially absent. The editing results (Fig. 5, 6, 19, 20) are qualitative only, and the paper itself acknowledges that the editing model is limited by CLIP's single input embedding, offering limited identity preservation. No editing metrics or user study are provided to substantiate the editing claims.

The comparison set omits several recent 2025 methods and some competitive baselines. In addition, the method does not consistently win on all metrics (e.g., GAGAvatar achieves higher SSIM on Ava-256 and NeRSemble), and the paper does not fully discuss these trade-offs beyond asserting that its metrics are 'better aligned with human perceptual quality.'

The proposed perceptual loss depends on very large frozen foundation models (DINOv2 ViT-g/14 with four feature maps, plus SAM 2.1). While Tab. 5 reports some memory/forward costs for a lightweight variant, the memory and inference cost of the full proposed pipeline (including the 3D decoder and SAM 2.1 loss) during training is not fully characterized, which is relevant for reproducibility and practical use.

Some claims are only weakly substantiated by the evidence presented: the assertion of 'state-of-the-art' is based on a limited baseline set, and the video/expression results (Fig. 4) are acknowledged to introduce flickering in unobserved regions, with the full video only in supplementary material rather than quantitatively analyzed.

Minor methodological reporting gaps: the loss weights (lambda_D = lambda_S = 1.0) and layer choices (L = {8, 11}) are stated but the rationale for these specific values/layers is only partially justified, and the interaction between the DINOv2 and SAM 2.1 terms is not analyzed beyond the combined ablation.

strengths: The core contribution—replacing conventional low-level image losses (L1, LPIPS, SSIM) with a perceptual loss built on DINOv2 mid/late-layer activations plus SAM 2.1 encodings—is well-motivated, genuinely useful, and convincingly supported by the ablations in Tab. 2 and Fig. 8/9. The finding that foundation-model features provide sufficient (and better) supervision for high-frequency regions like hair and glasses is a meaningful result that challenges a common assumption in the field.

Quantitative results are strong and consistent across two benchmarks. On Ava-256 the method leads on PSNR (16.4/15.9), LPIPS (0.269/0.291), DreamSim (0.092/0.106) and ArcFace (0.292/0.282) for both novel and extreme views, and Tab. 3 shows the same pattern on NeRSemble. The gains are most pronounced exactly where prior work is weakest—extreme/side viewpoints—which is the paper's stated target.

Evaluation breadth is good: two multi-view datasets (Ava-256, NeRSemble) plus in-the-wild FFHQ and diffusion-generated inputs (SORA), with a robustness analysis and a lightweight-variant study (Tab. 5) that reports compute and memory. This makes the claims about generalization more credible than a single-benchmark result.

The architecture description is clear enough to follow the key design decisions (dual-branch DINOv2+ViT encoder, FLAME-anchored 3D latent decoder with cross-attention to 2D features, PixelShuffle to Gaussians, SHP-CNN sharpening), and the editing extension (segmentation map for geometry, CLIP/reference image for style) is a natural and useful reuse of the base model.

The paper is honest about limitations (no expression transfer, no temporal understanding, baked-in lighting) and includes an interactive GUI and released code/website, which supports reproducibility and practical usefulness.

Ablations are thoughtfully designed, including data variants (2D only, multi-view only, combined), loss variants, SHP-CNN, and a patch-vs-class-token analysis in the supplement, all of which isolate the contribution of individual components.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental at the architectural level: the encoder–decoder design, FLAME anchor initialization, cross-attention to 2D features, and Gaussian Splatting head representation are closely related to LAM [28] and other recent Gaussian avatar works. The main new element is the perceptual loss, so the contribution rests heavily on that one component.

The perceptual loss itself builds on a known direction (DINOv2-based losses appear in prior work such as [46, 62, 72, 75]); the specific DINOv2+SAM2.1 combination is new but the paper does not fully delineate how it differs in formulation from these existing DINO-based perceptual losses beyond layer/feature choices.

Editing quality is evaluated almost entirely qualitatively (Figs. 5, 6, 7, 19, 20). There is no quantitative metric for edit fidelity, identity preservation under editing, or geometry/style disentanglement, which weakens the editing claims relative to the well-quantified reconstruction results.

The loss weighting (λD = λS = 1.0) and the layer choices (layers 8 and 11) are stated but not ablated in the main paper; the supplement examines layers for early training but the final selection rationale is only partially justified, and sensitivity to these choices is unclear.

SSIM is not the best (GAGAvatar is higher on both settings), and the paper argues this metric is less aligned with perceptual quality—a reasonable argument, but the discussion would be stronger with a perceptual user study rather than relying solely on DreamSim/ArcFace as proxies.

SHP-CNN is a somewhat ad-hoc post-hoc sharpening module with modest quantitative effect (Tab. 2 shows it mainly improves LPIPS/DreamSim), and its interaction with the perceptual loss is not deeply analyzed.

The method cannot relight or transfer expressions and exhibits flickering in video, which limits applicability to the avatar animation use cases the introduction motivates; these are acknowledged but represent real functional gaps.

strengths: The proposed perceptual loss (DINOv2 mid-to-late layer patch+class tokens combined with SAM 2.1 image encodings) is well motivated and empirically justified: Table 2/Fig. 8–9 show that LPIPS+L1 or either component alone yields blurry hair, missing glasses/teeth, or color casts, while the combined loss gives the best DreamSim (0.106 vs. 0.115 for LPIPS+L1) and ArcFace (0.282 vs. 0.300), and the early-epoch visualization convincingly shows faster recovery of glasses/hair/teeth.

Quantitative results are strong and consistent on two unseen benchmarks (Ava-256 and held-out NeRSemble identities) across PSNR, LPIPS, DreamSim and ArcFace, including the difficult extreme-view setting (e.g., Ava-256 extreme: PSNR 15.9 vs. 14.3 for SphereHead, LPIPS 0.291 vs. 0.349; NeRSemble extreme: 17.7 PSNR, 0.221 LPIPS), and the gains are reported against recent strong baselines (LAM, GAGAvatar, PanoHead, SphereHead, LGM).

The ablation and analysis section is thorough and useful: training-data mixture (2D-only data collapses to 6.5 PSNR, showing the multi-view data is essential), loss variants, DINOv2 layer selection, patch-vs-class-token supervision (Fig. 10), SH-CNN on/off, lightweight model variants with compute/memory in Table 5, and careful evaluation-protocol alignment (unified cropping, GAGAvatar background replacement).

Beyond reconstruction, the method supports genuinely useful downstream functionality: geometry via FaRL segmentation maps, style via reference image or CLIP text prompt (zero-shot), an interactive GUI/web application, and demonstrated robustness to in-the-wild FFHQ samples and stylized/generated inputs (Figs. 15–18), with code and GUI promised.

The paper is largely honest about its limits: it reports the cases where baselines win (GAGAvatar's higher SSIM), acknowledges the CLIP-based style limitation on identity preservation, and explicitly lists limitations (no expression transfer, no temporal model, baked-in lighting, flicker in video).
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is limited. The backbone (dual-branch DINOv2/ViT 2D encoder, FLAME-anchored Gaussian patches, 3D ViT decoder with cross-attention to 2D features) is explicitly described as following LAM [28]; the new elements are the loss combination and an encoder swap for editing. The paper's main claim to novelty therefore rests on the loss, which is itself a combination of two off-the-shelf foundation models.

There is a plausible circularity in the perceptual evaluation: the model is trained with a DINOv2-feature loss and then judged largely with DreamSim (DINOv2-based) and LPIPS (deep-feature-based). Improvements on these metrics are therefore not independent evidence of perceptual quality, and no user study is provided to support the central claim of improved perceptual realism and identity preservation.

The SH-CNN sharpening module looks like a metric-targeted post-process: per Table 2 it changes only LPIPS (0.301 → 0.291) and DreamSim (0.116 → 0.106) while leaving PSNR and ArcFace exactly unchanged (15.9, 0.282). It is trained against a DINOv2 class token and applied only to the proposed method, not to the baselines, so part of the perceptual-metric advantage in Table 1 may reflect this module rather than a more faithful reconstruction.

The editing contribution, which is a headline in the title, is evaluated only qualitatively (Figs. 5–7, 19–20). There is no quantitative benchmark, no comparison against text/image editing baselines except a single qualitative comparison to NeRFaceEditing (Fig. 7), and no user study. Claims of robust zero-shot text editing and geometry/style disentanglement are illustrated with a small number of curated examples (some of which, e.g., the 'female with curly hair' / 'male with gray beard' rows in Fig. 5 and the geometry column changes in Fig. 20, suggest noticeable geometry variation across prompts), so disentanglement is asserted rather than measured.

Evaluation breadth and protocol clarity are limited: quantitative results rest on a small set of unseen subjects (5 NeRSemble identities; the ~11 Ava-256 IDs listed in Supp. F.1), and the extreme-view protocol ('the corresponding opposing horizontal view') is never precisely defined in terms of angle range or whether back-of-head views are included, which makes the headline robustness claim hard to verify or reproduce.

Several cited generalizable 3D head/Gaussian methods (e.g., GGHead [35], Portrait4D [12]) are discussed but not compared quantitatively, and FaceLift is moved to the supplementary (Supp. C.1) rather than reported in the main table, weakening the completeness of the main comparison.

Minor consistency issues: the text claims the method 'consistently outperforms all baselines' in Sec. 4.2 while simultaneously conceding GAGAvatar's higher SSIM (0.743 vs. 0.691 novel; 0.694 vs. 0.678 extreme) without explanation, and Table 5's header appears to omit the PSNR column.
